column5: moisture-laden cloud and lightning cloud
column6: The commentary singles out weak lightning at the cloud’s edges before rain; Job describes God loading the cloud with moisture and scattering the cloud of his light, keeping those two features together.

column5: drops drawn up and rain distilled from mist
column6: The commentary fills the unspoken interval from cloud to rain; Job describes the water cycle as God drawing up drops and distilling rain from mist.

column5: God visiting and richly watering earth
column6: The commentary calls rain the life of earth that produces pasture; this psalm says God visits the earth, waters it, and greatly enriches it in preparation for grain.

column5: furrows softened by showers and growth blessed
column6: The commentary’s first rain leaves a visible green mark in the soil; the psalm describes water in furrows, showers softening ridges, and God blessing the earth’s growth.

column5: wilderness pastures overflowing
column6: The commentary treats marʿā as grass and pasture-place, not an abstract crop; after the rain imagery this psalm says the wilderness pastures overflow with abundance.

column5: rains in season, land yield, tree fruit
column6: The commentary makes seasonal rain the cause of pasture’s first appearance; the covenant blessing promises rains in their season, land produce, and fruit from field trees.

column5: rain for seed and broad pasture for cattle
column6: The commentary joins rain, ground-emergence, and the feeding sense of pasture; Isaiah promises rain for sown seed, rich produce, and cattle grazing in a broad pasture.

column5: showers of blessing on fields and trees
column6: The commentary’s nurturing Lord is heard in a cloud that feeds plants; Ezekiel calls the timely rain “showers of blessing” and immediately has field trees yield their fruit.

column5: wilderness pastures sprouting
column6: The commentary tracks the pasture from first green emergence onward; Joel tells the animals not to fear because the wilderness pastures have sprouted and the trees bear fruit.

column5: cloud rising and a coming shower
column6: The commentary dwells on the cloud’s first appearance as a sign that rain will come; Jesus describes observers seeing a cloud rise in the west and correctly expecting a shower.

column5: south wind and expected heat
column6: The commentary gives the south wind a secondary role beside the cloud; Jesus likewise uses the south wind as a recognized weather sign, here for scorching heat.

column5: shallow soil causing quick sprouting
column6: The commentary notes first green appearing only in some patches of earth; in the sower parable seed on shallow rocky soil springs up immediately because the soil has no depth.

column5: sun-scorched, rootless growth withering
column6: The commentary follows fresh green into dried refuse; the parable’s quickly sprouted plant is scorched by the sun and withers because it has no root.

column5: still-green plant withering before others
column6: The commentary makes aḥwā hold lush green darkness beside the blackened end of vegetation; Job’s plant is still green and uncut when it withers before other plants.

column5: plant struck and withered
column6: The commentary stresses that the same creator who brings out pasture turns it into a later state; Jonah’s God appoints a worm to strike the sheltering plant, and it withers.

column5: east wind making a growing vine wither
column6: The commentary assigns wind a role in the cloud-and-grass sequence and ends with dried vegetation; Ezekiel’s vine is flourishing until an east wind strikes it and makes it wither where it grew.

column5: morning mist, dew, wind-driven chaff, smoke
column6: The commentary moves from cloud and first moisture to plant-debris, then notes that such debris can figure people; Hosea describes the guilty as morning mist, vanishing dew, whirlwind-driven chaff, and smoke.

column5: full clouds emptying rain on earth
column6: The commentary infers rain as the causal middle between cloud and pasture; Qoheleth states the connection plainly: clouds full of rain empty it on the earth.

column5: watching wind and clouds instead of sowing and reaping
column6: The commentary imagines someone spending the night watching lightning to learn where it will flash; Qoheleth turns weather-observation into an agricultural warning, since one who watches wind will not sow and one who looks at clouds will not reap.

column5: Most High, shelter, and shadow
column6: The commentary calls the Lord “Most High” and defines the sky by its overarching shade; this psalm places the one dwelling in the shelter of the Most High in the shadow of the Almighty.

column5: high exaltation and name above every name
column6: The commentary’s first command joins the divine name to highestness; Paul says God highly exalted Jesus and granted him the name above every name.

column5: well-watered garden and unfailing spring
column6: The commentary contrasts ordinary grass that dries with plants that escape summer death; Isaiah promises a well-watered garden and a spring whose water does not fail.

column5: tree of life with unceasing fruit and healing leaves
column6: The commentary sets darkened, dried pasture beside the Qur’anic image of enduring lush gardens; Revelation’s final garden has the tree of life yielding fruit each month and leaves for healing.

column5: hidden face, death, and return to dust
column6: The commentary pairs S87:7’s hiddenness with S87:13’s death and life; this psalm says that when God hides his face creatures are dismayed, lose breath, die, and return to dust.

column5: sent breath creating and renewing the ground
column6: The commentary makes earth’s rain-borne life a bridge to restoration; the answering verse has God send breath, create living beings, and renew the face of the ground.

column5: desolate land cultivated again
column6: The commentary defines dead land as land not yet made alive by sowing or repair; Ezekiel says the desolate land will be cultivated instead of lying desolate.

column5: desolate land becoming the garden of Eden
column6: The commentary’s green-to-black scene also holds the possibility of a contrary garden; Ezekiel’s restored land is compared to Eden after its devastated places are rebuilt.

column5: perishing heaven and earth, everlasting salvation
column6: The commentary begins with sky and ends by weighing the passing world against what endures; Isaiah says heaven vanishes and earth wears out, while God’s salvation is forever.

column5: better and abiding possession
column6: The commentary highlights S87:17’s claim that the future is both better and more lasting; Hebrews uses the same paired valuation when it speaks of a better and abiding possession.

column5: weeds gathered and burned at the end of the age
column6: The commentary notes that the Qur’an can transfer vegetative debris to human communities and then reaches the great fire; Jesus’ interpretation transfers weeds into people gathered for burning at the age’s end.

column5: fiery furnace and conscious grief
column6: The commentary’s fire-state is a human fate after the plant image; Jesus’ sequel says the evildoers are thrown into a fiery furnace, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth.

column5: branch not abiding, withering, gathered for fire
column6: The commentary contrasts the pasture’s fleeting life with what remains and then turns to fire; Jesus says a branch that does not abide is thrown out, withers, is gathered, and burned.

column5: eternal punishment and eternal life
column6: The commentary’s “neither dies nor lives” in great fire is set against a better enduring hereafter; Jesus’ final judgment explicitly divides people between eternal punishment and eternal life.

column5: leaves falling and new leaves growing
column6: The commentary makes the complete plant life-cycle interpret human mortality; Sirach compares generations of flesh and blood to a tree whose leaves fall while others grow.

column5: sowing to corruption or eternal life
column6: The commentary’s pasture becomes a moral contrast between passing life and what endures; Paul’s sowing image makes flesh reap corruption and Spirit reap eternal life.

column5: fallow ground broken for righteousness
column6: The commentary calls unseeded, unrepaired soil “dead land”; Hosea turns breaking fallow ground, sowing, and reaping into an ethical summons to seek YHWH.

column5: water becoming a spring of eternal life
column6: The commentary calls rain life because it brings life to earth; Jesus recasts given water as a spring welling up to eternal life, shifting the image to a person’s lasting life.

column5: hidden things of darkness brought to light
column6: The commentary combines God’s knowledge of hidden things with faint light in cloud; Paul says the Lord will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and disclose the heart’s purposes.

column5: soul like a watered garden, no longer languishing
column6: The commentary opposes dried pasture to an undying green state; Jeremiah describes restored Israel’s life as a watered garden that will languish no more.

column5: seasonal mention of the power of rain
column6: The commentary names the first rain and treats rain as a bridge toward the life/death horizon; the Mishnah debates when the “power of rain” begins to be mentioned in communal seasonal prayer.

column5: ungodly hope swept like light chaff or froth
column6: The commentary’s ghuthā is dry debris carried away and can figure people; Wisdom similarly compares the ungodly’s hope to light material driven off by wind and storm, though English renderings vary in the precise plant term.
